text: Data Structures was a rough ride this semester. I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the organization felt chaotic—the schedule never seemed to align with what we actually had to turn in, and the platform glitches jumbled deadlines in a way that helped nobody, especially when we hit a week with three due dates. My strong coding background got me through most of the hard parts, but the theory felt thin and dry, and the forums could be helpful yet occasionally dismissive, which didn’t motivate me to ask follow-ups. I remember one early confusion about pointers that cascaded into a few late nights chasing an answer, and that shapes how I view the rest of the term even now.

Starting the Machine Learning course mid‑semester, I was juggling a full-time job, so I appreciated the moment the office hours finally clicked for me—the quick problem fixes saved a week of scrambled tries. The tool setup felt like a slog and the heavy report workload didn’t help, but the content at least hooked me enough to keep going; it’s strongest if you’ve already crossed into adjacent material. A late turning point helped me push through, even though attendance faded earlier and the deadlines piled up.

I took Database Systems mid-program core expecting it to be useful for industry work, and it mostly delivered, especially once I could batch short evening study sessions around a couple of weeks when deadlines stacked up unexpectedly. I started off engaged but attendance faded mid-semester as workload piled on and the pacing felt uneven; the recorded lectures are handy, but they come across as dry unless I rewatch with a concrete problem in mind. The platform quirks added avoidable stress—little things like needing a separate login for the quiz tool and the auto-save sometimes not kicking in when I needed it most, which bummed me out after a long day. Some feedback from the instructor showed up too late to help right when I needed it, so I relied on classmates more than staff to hash out tricky queries. I did enjoy the hands-on vibe of the project, especially coding the simple query planner in the final week, though the deadlines were stacked, and I felt rushed. Overall I’d still recommend broadly, since the core ideas feel solid and relevant, even if the delivery had its rough edges.

Calculus II was a mid-semester slog for me, and I mostly relied on recordings and notes because the live lectures didn’t grab me. The slides are serviceable but not memorable, and I felt like I needed more prior intuition than the course advertised, so I had to scramble to connect the dots on my own. Group work helped when our team actually communicated, though that didn’t happen every week. Office hours were the real rescue, especially when I kept looping on the integration by parts patterns and finally got a clear explanation during a 20-minute chat. I wouldn’t take it again, even though it did push me to focus on this term as my main course.

Data Structures was my last year requirement for the track, and I’m still surprised how much I stuck with it after I barely knew the basics at first. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, and timing on feedback dragged—until I finally showed up to office hours and got roots-level clarifications that rescued the course for me, especially around array vs linked-list thinking; that small moment helped me push through a tricky project.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester, juggling Cyber Security Basics with a couple other tough courses, and I mostly used the materials only when I needed them. The platform has quirks that create avoidable stress—like the annoying nav hiccups right before a deadline and the way files don’t always load correctly on my side, which didn’t help when I was scrambling to keep up. The course is assignment-heavy with frequent deadlines, and while the grading comments are detailed, they arrive a bit late, which stings when I’m staring at a looming due date. I genuinely like the instructor and the way they frame security concepts, but I wish the feedback came faster so I could actually apply it to the next submission. I heard it would be useful for industry work, and parts of the project (a small, hands-on packet analyze-and-flag task) helped in that sense, but the experience felt uneven because I only watched the materials selectively, used the tools when needed, and still felt rushed. Overall, it’s solid but the timing and the platform quirks left a persistent ripple.

Data Structures felt like something I was supposed to know better than I did, since I was new to the discipline and still learning the basics, but it’s a required elective so I pressed on. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, which helped keep the plateaus of motivation from crumbling too much on weeks I felt tired and dragged my feet. I’d say the prerequisite expectation was a bit too high for me—there’s talk of graph algorithms and memory structures that felt assumed, even though the course didn’t clearly bridge that gap for someone like me. By the late semester turning point, I felt a chill of “I should have started earlier,” and feedback arrived too late to be useful for the big final project, though the occasional peer comment helped a touch.

I came away with a mixed, unsettled sense about the Machine Learning core course this term. It became the main focus for me, but the organization felt rough—instructions left a lot up to interpretation, and the software stack was bumpy at first before it finally started to click. I kept a lot of the materials on the side, using them only when a deadline loomed, which made the semester feel like a mid-semester crunch rather than steady progress. The grading was heavy on reports and there were moments where I wasn’t sure if the score reflected true understanding, especially since I scrambled to meet tight, repeated deadlines and emails for support dragged. Overall, it was doable but not smoothly so, and I still feel unsure how much I actually internalized.

The course felt like a mixed bag from the start, and I’m still torn about whether I’d sign up again, even though I did learn a lot. The material was mostly solid and the lectures were packed with code demos that kept me awake, especially the hands-on notebook sessions; the LMS and submission flow were smooth enough to not add stress on top of everything else. I kept up with nearly every lecture, but the structure left a lot of room for interpretation in the instructions, which made some assignments feel like tests of guessing what the grader wanted rather than a clear rubric. It was an assignment-heavy environment with frequent deadlines, and the fast feedback was nice—scores came quickly, but the explanations were thin, so I didn’t always know what to fix. One concrete hiccup sticks: a project due right after spring break, where the expectations felt broader than the brief suggested, and I spent more time rereading guidelines than coding. I’d say the course helped me in a few ways, but I’d also be exhausted if I were to do it again in this form.

I’m in the last semester before graduation, slogging through Data Structures with Prof. Rios, and I actually found the lectures pretty clear despite the crunch at midterm. The pacing felt reasonable when I could keep up, and the course is clearly a required piece for the track, so you’re pushing through even if the prerequisites feel heavier than advertised. The workload is very report-heavy and time-consuming, which didn’t help during the mid-semester sprint, but I’ll admit the fast arrival of scores helped a bit—though the explanations were thin. I compared it to another course from the same term and, honestly, the exam felt fair but demanded more prior fluency than I expected; my solid B fit the effort I put in, even if I’m still unsure about some design-frontier questions.

Calculus II felt like it came in fits and starts, especially since I’m juggling short evening study sessions and I’m coming back to math after a while, so I was rusty and uncertain about whether the work reflected how much I actually understood. The lectures explained concepts well enough, but the examples were thin and the assessment mix didn’t quite line up with what we covered in class, which left me guessing a lot. The quick feedback on grades was nice—scores arrived fast, but the explanations were thin and didn’t always tell me what to fix next. Still, the organization kept things moving, and I’d say I’d probably recommend it to others who need the credit, even if I wouldn’t take it again myself.

Cyber Security Basics was a solid intro, I started off really engaged but my attendance faded mid-semester as evenings got busier; the LMS felt smooth and the project-heavy flow kept me chasing the deadline pattern, though collaboration felt a bit unclear.

I took Linear Algebra with Prof. Haddad while juggling a full-time job, and the pace in the middle of a heavy semester felt relentless, especially as deadlines stacked up unexpectedly. The quick feedback helped me adjust, but email support was slow when a major assignment was due, which was annoying. The course builds well on the prerequisites, though the assessment mix often felt off compared to what we actually covered in lectures, like a midterm that didn’t align with our weekly problem sets. Still, a concrete moment—the group project using matrix factorization—stuck with me, even if I worried I wasn’t spending enough time on the theory side.

I started the Data Structures course with a decent coding background, but the theory side felt thin and the ramp-up was sharp, especially since the platform and tooling were rough at first. I liked the schedule, but deadlines piled up oddly and the collaboration expectations felt unclear, so I found myself juggling unclear groups and misaligned assessments more than I expected. By midsemester my attendance faded a bit, and I ended up learning a lot yet not enjoying the overall experience. The project on a binary tree analysis was memorable, but the whole thing left me with mixed feelings.

The Database Systems course was a tougher fit for a summer term with compressed pacing, but honestly the difficulty level pushed me in a good way and I kept up by juggling it with two other heavy courses. I appreciated that the material stuck, and the late-semester turning point around the final project finally clicked into place, even if the tool setup and initial prerequisites felt heavier than advertised. The forums helped when I needed quick clarifications, though I noticed some dismissive vibes there that slowed me down at times. I wouldn’t take it again, but it did push my boundaries and the solid B I earned matched the effort I put in. Overall, I’d say it’s a real, imperfect fit for an intro service course.

took machine learning in my last semester, and it felt useful more than enjoyable. the explanations were strong on the concepts, but the examples often felt thin, like we sketched the intuition and then moved on. deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and the assignment-heavy weeks with frequent due dates made it hard to pace around my short evening study sessions, so i picked through the readings only when i needed a concrete idea for a problem. i’d say the fast feedback on scores helped keep me moving, but the explanations behind the marks were thin, which left me wondering what to tighten next time. one concrete moment: a late-night project submission window glitch caused a last-minute scramble to re-run a binomial classifier, which stuck with me as a reminder to double-check the due dates.

The Computer Networks class was a rough ride but overall worth sticking with in my first semester. Recorded lectures helped when I fell behind, though they could feel dry, and the software stack started rough but got manageable. I burned through deadlines to catch up, and the-heavy, report-driven assessments ate time, leaving me tired and unsure about how well I was actually keeping up. My midterm week still sticks in memory, honestly.

Cyber Security Basics started off with a lot of promise for someone like me who’s comfortable with proofs but not systems work, but the practical reality quickly felt heavier than the syllabus suggested. I appreciated the relevance of the topics, especially the way the course tried to connect theory to real threat models, yet the overall experience suffered from tooling issues that made every deadline week feel like dragging through mud. Dr. Park is clearly thoughtful and offers detailed, sometimes granular feedback, but the grading comments tend to arrive late, which makes it hard to adjust midstream or learn from mistakes in time. The course is very report-heavy and time-consuming, and I kept falling behind around deadlines only to scramble back up at the last minute, which didn’t help the sense of progress. Office hours were a lifeline, genuinely rescuing the course when I needed quick clarifications, though it’s not a reliable daily support channel. If I compare this to the easier prerequisite I took earlier, this one felt more data- and formatting-driven than substance-driven, and the one standout memory week was the midterm where a single tricky assignment dragged out across two nights. I can’t fully recommend it despite some value, and the experience could have been smoother with more consistent tooling and timelier feedback.

I’m new to the discipline and juggling a full-time job, so Linear Algebra felt like a test of stamina as much as brains, especially in the middle of a heavy semester. The lecturer was clearly knowledgeable and kept explanations practical, which helped a lot when I was trying to map abstract ideas to a real-world data project I was squeezing in between shifts. I’d get quick feedback on quizzes, but the reasoning behind why one step was marked wrong sometimes felt thin, which left me doubting whether I’d fully internalized the method or just memorized a workaround. The forums helped occasionally, though some threads came off as dismissive, like you should already know what you’re doing, which isn’t comforting when you’re learning from scratch. The grading rubric is vague, and the heavy report-style assessments drain evenings that should be for sleep; I ended up rushing parts just to hit the deadline patterns I noticed, rather than feeling confident about the conclusions. Compared to another course I took in the same term, this one demanded more time on documentation than on intuition, and I both learned a lot and still felt frustrated by the overall flow. The standout moment? a midterm problem about eigenvectors that I finally sort of grokked, but the process left me exhausted and unsure if I’d be ready for the next step.

Dr. Singh’s Linear Algebra was solid in clarity and pace, especially compared to the easier prereqs I’ve survived, and I appreciated how his lectures tied the concepts to the notes I could skim during a busy week. I mainly relied on recordings and discussion with peers to fill gaps, since the official materials sometimes felt sparse, and while the grading comments are thorough, they tend to show up a bit late, which slowed my midterm prep.

I took Machine Learning mostly out of genuine curiosity, kept up with nearly every lecture, and tried to balance it with a couple of other demanding courses, which made the workload feel manageable most weeks but still a bit constant. The design of the assessments felt fair in the sense that there was a steady path to show progress, and the quick feedback helped me adjust my approach as we went. Where I got annoyed was how the tool setup for the course took more time than the actual learning, so I ended up chasing environments rather than chasing ideas. The course works best if you have a study group, because parsing the lecture examples and clarifying the intuition after class helped a lot, especially when the slides skipped steps. The lectures themselves sometimes left me frustrated about the pace and the level of detail, and I found myself comparing this to the expectations I had going in rather than to another course. Overall it felt useful but not enjoyable, and I’m not sure I’d recommend it despite some value. The final takeaway is a mixed sense of momentum and friction, with a project deadline that sticks in my memory as emblematic of the steady grind.

Looking back on Cyber Security Basics, I’m still surprised how much the early confusion stuck with me and colored the rest of the term: I remember realizing in week two that I had been mixing up risk assessment with threat modeling, which made the first few weeks feel like I was running in circles. I was juggling full-time work, so I fit study around short evening sessions, and the deadlines piled up in a way that felt brutal when tooling glitches ate into the week’s momentum. The course definitely works better with a study group; alone I felt the report-heavy tasks stretched out forever, but bouncing ideas off two classmates helped me catch some mistakes even if we still argued about whether a metric mattered. I’m not sure I’d happily recommend it, since the policy side seemed fine in theory but communication felt sloppy at times, and the weekly deadline pattern sometimes turned into a sprint with last-minute polish. One standout moment was a late-night pull request where the tooling error flipped a graph and I nearly failed to notice it—the shock stuck with me and shaped how I approached the rest of the term, more cautious and slower but somehow determined.

Linear Algebra felt clear in lectures but the overall grasp was shaky, and I still mix up eigenvectors with my notes. I mainly relied on recordings, and I remember one office hours session where the TA finally explained a tricky matrix diag process, which helped a bit.

I stuck with almost every lecture, since the proofs vibe felt easier than the system stuff, but the prerequisites didn’t really align with what we did; the late, detailed grading comments helped a bit, and the group work sometimes clicked when our team actually synchronized.

Midway through the heavy semester, I’m glad the prerequisites for Cyber Security Basics still feel like they fit, and Dr. Park builds on them well, even if the lectures don’t always spark joy. I used the materials selectively, and peer discussions helped more than the official stuff; the few assessments mattered a lot, and the feedback so far has felt sparse until it was basically too late, which left me with mixed, conflicted vibes. One memorable week was the alarming mock exam that caught me off guard, and I’m not sure I’d recommend the course without being prepared.

I stuck with Computer Networks mostly because it fit my schedule better than my interest in the topic, and I kept up with nearly every lecture even though motivation sometimes wandered. The course had moments where tooling hiccups made deadlines feel weeks longer than they actually were, and feedback arrived too late to really help me adjust before the next assignment. I remember an early confusion around subnetting that made the rest of the term feel like I was fighting an uphill climb, even though the TAs were responsive and practical when I emailed. Prof. Rios graded with detail, but the comments showed up after the next due date, which was kind of frustrating.

Data Structures with Dr. Chen was required for my degree, so I showed up mostly because I had to, not because I was buzzing with enthusiasm. The materials were solid in principle and I appreciated the clean slides and the quick lookup guides, which I used only when I needed a refresher, since the lectures didn’t always click for me week to week. I found the instruction uneven—some weeks felt like we were sprinting through topics, other weeks it dragged and left questions hanging without clear guidance, which didn’t help since the feedback timing is fast but the explanations are thin. The administrative side left a bit of interpretation up for grabs, and I ended up chasing what “requirements” meant as the deadlines stacked up; I remember one week where the lab handout seemed to imply two different approaches. I mostly worked on my own, with the occasional consult at office hours or a quick forum thread, and I’m still unsure whether my C reflected true understanding or just a rough grasp of the material. One memorable moment was the week of the midterm where a tricky data-structure twist caught a lot of us off guard. Overall, the course felt more accessible than I fearfully expected, even if the delivery wasn’t consistently tight.

The Data Structures course felt solid for me this summer, with clear lectures that kept a decent pace and a project-heavy setup that matched the effort I put in. I appreciated the lecturer’s steady explanations, though the communication from admin felt a bit sloppy at times, especially around deadline tweaks. I compared it to the easier prerequisite and still felt the workload was fair, even as I was juggling another hard class and sometimes dragged by inconsistent motivation.

Starting the first semester, I leaned on recordings and notes more than live lectures, since the pace and some platform quirks left me chasing the right slides more than the discussion. My strong coding background helped, but the theory bits still tripped me up at first: I remember an early confusion about overfitting that colored how I approached the rest of the term. Forums helped sometimes, though a few threads felt dismissive, and you really want a study group to make the workload feel manageable.

Dr. Park’s Database Systems was solid but demanding, and I kept up with nearly every lecture while juggling a full-time job. I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and the course ramps up quickly after the accessible intro, with a heavy assignment load and tight deadlines; office hours saved me more than once when I was stuck on a SQL design problem. I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared to push through and stay ahead of the clock.

Data Structures was a solid ride in the middle of a brutal semester, honestly. I stuck with it when I could, but attendance faded as deadlines piled up, and I relied on a few TA hours and forum threads more than staff help; the grading felt tight—fast scores but thin explanations—yet the project utils and the midterm format kept me honest. The instructor felt a bit uneven week to week, but I still learned enough to push through.

Signed up for Database Systems mid‑semester and I’m still unsure if I really grok the core concepts. The lecturer can explain ideas well at a high level, but the concrete examples were thin, which didn’t help when I hit a tricky indexing problem early on and felt lost for a few days. I mostly relied on recordings and notes, since live lectures felt fast and a lot of the tooling felt fiddly to use, especially when the diagramming tool hiccuped during group work. The few assessments count a lot, and a single project deadline kept getting moved, which didn’t help my shaky start. By the end I guess the prerequisite gaps were better filled than I expected, but I’m still unsure whether the grade reflects true understanding. The team could click when everyone pulled their weight, though.

Calculus II was a last‑semester hurdle I slogged through while juggling a full-time job; the work piled up fast, with frequent deadlines, and I felt the grading transparency was rough, but I did rely on study groups more than staff.

I’m glad I took Database Systems mainly because the professor explains the concepts clearly, even if the examples feel a bit thin at times, and I’m someone who’s comfortable with proofs but not really a “systems” person, so I appreciated the big-picture explanations more than the nitty-gritty debugging. The materials helped when I needed to check a proof-of-join idea, but the platform and tooling setup was rough at first and I spent more time fiddling with environments than actually coding queries, which was frustrating since the admin friction dragged out a lot of early momentum. The exams felt unfair to me in how they framed questions—like they tested obscure edge cases rather than the practical understanding I expected from a required track course—so I left with a sense of unease about how to study for them. I did like that the coursework felt useful in the long run, even if I didn’t enjoy it day-to-day, and I mostly worked solo with the occasional reliance on the lecture notes when I needed a reminder about a concept instead of hunting down a peer to discuss it. There was a tiny incident with a deadline pattern that threw me off for a day, but otherwise the core ideas about data modeling and abstraction stuck, and I can see how it connects to real projects, even if I wouldn’t call it my favorite class.

Database Systems in my first semester felt relevant, especially since I was juggling a full-time job at the same time. Dr. Chen’s lectures were there, but the recorded videos were dry enough that I often paused to rewatch a section and hope my brain would wake up before the quiz. The feedback came quickly, which helped a bit, but the explanations behind the scores were thin, so I spent more time chasing what I did wrong than applying what I learned. Office hours were a lifesaver—someone finally walked me through SQL join pitfalls I kept tripping on—yet the prerequisite vibe felt off, like there was more hidden knowledge than the ad copy suggested. Deadlines stacked up oddly, and by the time finals rolled around I barely passed, still not feeling sure I could set up a proper database project without fumbling.

Database Systems with Dr. Singh was solid for me, especially since I’m comfortable with proofs but not systems work; office hours saved the week I froze on indexing, and the early confusion about query plans shaped how I approached the rest despite uneven weeks.

I took Cyber Security Basics this summer, and I’m still not sure I’d call it thrilling, but Prof. Rios kept things moving despite the compressed pacing. The lectures were serviceable—slides got the point across, but they didn’t linger in memory, and I’m someone who’s comfortable with proofs rather than systems work, so the material felt a bit rushed to connect for me. Quick feedback helped me adjust before the next week, which was nice, though the collaboration expectations still felt unclear and I wasn’t sure who was coordinating what in our group. One small concrete snag: we had a recurring deadline pattern that sometimes hit right after a lab, which mattered more than I expected, and I sometimes questioned whether the grading matched the effort, even though the instructor was approachable. Overall, it was fine, just not the standout course I hoped for.

Calculus II was an advanced elective I took because it was required for the degree, and I kept up with nearly every lecture, though I ended up feeling the grading rubric was vague and kinda frustrated by how little guidance there was on what actually mattered. The LMS and submission flow were smooth, but the few assessments felt heavy—one midterm and a final that seemed to decide a lot, with a rough mid‑semester crunch left me juggling deadlines. I’m mixed on it, and I wouldn’t call it a smooth ride, but I did learn something despite the blur.

I’m glad I stuck with Linear Algebra, but the workload felt punishing for an intro service course, especially since I came from a strong coding background and not much theory. The mid‑semester crunch loomed, the feedback was sparse until it was almost too late, and the tool setup demanded more effort than the payoff. Prof. Rios was genuinely enthusiastic, but the forums could be dismissive and the assessment exhausting even though it felt fair. I’d recommend it only if you’ve prepared to sprint through adjacent material first.

Taking the Operating Systems course this summer felt like sprinting through a book on a treadmill, since I’m juggling a full-time job and only have small pockets of study each week. I appreciated that the assessment design leaned into reports and data-heavy tasks, which matched the effort I could muster, but I kept bumping into the prerequisite gap—it assumed more prior knowledge than advertised, so I spent extra hours chasing concepts I felt should have been quick reviews. The lectures are recorded and I did find them useful, but they’re pretty dry, and I relied on the slides more than the talking, especially during the weeks with the five-page memory logs. My go-to interaction was emailing for clarifications when deadlines loomed, and, honestly, the response time felt slow enough to affect my pacing on a couple of big deliverables. I compared this term a bit to another course from the same term and the grading vibe there was lighter, so the heavy, time-sucking reports here stood out. The single memorable exam week—the one with the big memory map and two consecutive short essays—still sticks with me, even as I liked the instructor for clarity; I just wish the grading didn’t sting as much.

Calculus II, taken in a summer term while juggling other hard classes, built on the prerequisites but felt rushed. The forums helped at times, but responses could be dismissive; group work only clicked when our team actually synced. I remember a confusing integrals quiz and still have mixed feelings about the pace.

I stuck with almost every lecture for Machine Learning, and the pacing did feel steady, but the material was rougher than I hoped and the tool setup for experiments ate more time than the payoff. Prof. Rios’ recorded lectures helped when I felt stuck, though they’re pretty dry, and the assessments lately didn’t line up with what was emphasized in class. Email support was slow right before deadlines, which left me juggling a lot and wondering if the course was worth the extra effort compared to the other course I took this term.

I stuck with Database Systems because I had the time, but my motivation wandered mid-semester and attendance faded after a while. Prof. Rios’s lectures felt uneven week to week, and the forums could be helpful yet sometimes dismissive, which didn’t help my mood. The workload was heavy and report-heavy, yet it somehow fills the prerequisite gaps better than I expected, and the grade felt like a solid B for the effort I did. I remember one office-hours chat where I asked about a data-model question, and it didn't quite click, leaving me tired but with a sliver of clarity.

Taking the Operating Systems course this summer fit oddly well with my late-evening study blitzes, since the content moves fast enough to feel practical but not so dense that I’d drown after a long day. The group work mattered a lot when we lined up on the project sprint—our bossy, practical TA kept pushing us to ship something usable, and I actually used the disk scheduling tool from our lab in my side job interview prep. Deadlines were a steady trickle of pressure: big exams loomed, but the real value came from the hands-on projects that forced me to translate concepts into something I could point to in a chat with a teammate. I wouldn’t sign up again knowing the feedback comes late, and I’d prefer a bit more pace, but I did walk away feeling more confident in how to reason about systems under real-time constraints.

Data Structures with Prof. Cohen was my last-semester sprint, since I was new to the discipline I felt a bit behind early on and then somehow managed to catch up around deadlines. The slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I found the material mostly neutral to work through, with the tooling and online resources reasonable enough to get by; I appreciated the accessible setup when I needed a quick reference. I worked mostly solo, which matched my pace, though I wish the prerequisites had been a bit clearer—more prior exposure would have helped. Email support dragged when deadlines loomed, and I saw a lot of my own questions get answered only after I’d already adjusted my approach, which was frustrating but not fatal.

I’m new to the discipline, so Linear Algebra with Dr. Park felt like staring at a map I could almost read, especially during the summer term when pacing was tight and every concept came with a rushed reminder to “move on.” I mostly relied on the recordings and notes, and the LMS flow stayed smooth enough to not fight me on submissions, which helped since I’m juggling full-time work. The lectures didn’t always give me the full why behind techniques, but the office hours were a rescue: a couple of times I caught a gap in my intuition and left with a concrete, if thin, explanation that finally made sense of a stubborn problem. The collaboration was mostly solo work, so I didn’t lean on peers much, and I felt the structure supported that approach. Fast feedback on quizzes came with quick scores, though the explanations felt skimpy and I wished for a bit more example-driven reasoning. Compared to another course in the same term, Park’s pace felt more compressed, and I kept chasing a clearer thread between topics, yet the core ideas started to stick once I gripped a couple of crucial examples. One concrete memory: a late-week problem set that forced me to map a vector space to a simple real-world hint I could actually picture, which helped me tolerate the time squeeze. Overall, it’s a tradeoff course for me, with solid organization and access to help, but I’m not walking away with a polished intuition yet.

Took Data Structures with Prof. Alvarez during a summer term while working full‑time, so the pacing was compressed but still manageable if you form a study group. The class felt fair in its grading and the few big assessments mattered a lot, though feedback could swing from really helpful to a bit dismissive on some assignments. If I’m honest, the forums helped some days and left me frustrated on others, and I’ll remember that one exam week as both exhausting and oddly satisfying.

I’m juggling a full-time job, so I fit OS nights into short evening sessions and still feel like I’m chasing the material. Dr. Park is solid, but the software stack starts rough and only late in the semester does it settle into something manageable; TAs are quick and practical, though feedback sometimes arrives too late to help with the next deadline. I’d say it’s best if you’ve seen adjacent material already, and yes, I’d still recommend it broadly.

Machine Learning was a required hurdle in the middle of a brutal semester, and I walked out with an A after a curve, mostly because the material clicked despite the scattered feedback. The deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and tooling hiccups during week-long crunches made the report-heavy workload feel even heavier; one memorable exam week stuck in my mind as a sprint through model comparison questions, not long on guidance.

The Operating Systems course was tougher than I expected, but I’ll admit some parts clicked once I settled into the rhythm of the workload. I took it mainly because it’s required for the degree, and I have a pretty solid coding background, though I’m weaker on the theory side, so the jump from concepts to actual systems felt steep and sometimes frustratingly hand-wavy in lectures. The project-heavy setup plus high-stakes exams meant I could coast on practical work if I stayed up-to-date, but the timing of feedback was a mixed bag: scores came back fast, yet the explanations were thin and left me second-guessing where I went wrong. I found the TAs practical and responsive when I asked for help, which helped me salvage a few late nights, especially during the late-week lab sprint. One memory I still recall is the office-hours line where a TA sketched out a page table transition on the whiteboard and practically explained why my cache-mriendliness wasn’t helping my latency results. Overall, I can’t fully recommend it even though I learned a lot; the administration and interpretation-heavy instructions left too much room for confusion, and I ended the quarter feeling the curve masked how hard I’d actually worked.

Prof. Cohen’s Computer Networks was solid in lectures, and the forums helped, though some comments felt dismissive. I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and the mid‑semester crunch left me barely passing; the instructions left a lot open to interpretation, but a study group really helped.

Calculus II crept up in the middle of a brutal semester, and as a returning student who’s rusty, I found the lectures mostly dry but useful enough when I was cramming with the recordings and my notes between shifts at work. I’d say the biggest issue is the tooling and deadline weeks; every quiz or project felt like it needed some last-minute fiddling with the platform, which ate into study time I didn’t have, and the overall pacing didn’t help that sense of chaos. I did appreciate that the grading felt transparent enough when I actually looked at the rubric, even if I wasn’t totally convinced the numbers lined up with how solid my understanding seemed after I discussed problems in the TA office hours.
